blocks.content: Loess deposits create some of the world's most fertile agricultural soils, yet their loose structure makes them exceptionally vulnerable to erosion.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Loess consists of wind-blown silt particles deposited over vast areas far from their source region.
The Loess Plateau in China, drained by the Yellow River (Huang He), is the thickest and most extensive loess deposit globally.
Loess soils are exceptionally fertile due to rich mineral composition, high moisture retention, and easy root penetration.
Despite its agricultural richness, loess is structurally soft and highly susceptible to severe water and wind erosion.
Loess landscapes feature vertical cliffs and cave dwellings (Yaodongs) owing to its cohesive vertical cleavage property.
The Huang He is known as the 'Yellow River' primarily due to the vast amounts of yellow loess sediment it erodes and transports.
Loess is classified as an aeolian (wind-formed) landform that is fine-grained, unstratified, and dominated by quartz and silt.
Exams frequently test the vertical cohesive property of loess, which allows deep vertical cuts and cave habitations without structural failure.
